newsitem.title: HONG KONG: New Hong Kong party no supporter of Tung.
newsitem.headline: New Hong Kong party no supporter of Tung.

text.p: Hong Kong's newest political party, launched on Sunday just 58 days before the handover of the British colony to China, is shaping up to be another thorn in the side of future leader Tung Chee-hwa.
The driving force behind the new Citizens' Party, Christine Loh, is a vocal opponent of much of what Tung espouses.

Loh, a member of Hong Kong's legislature who stood as an independent in the 1995 polls, has no time for "Asian values" and has been active in opposing Tung's plans to roll back key clauses in Hong Kong's civil liberties laws.

Tung, who takes over from Governor Chris Patten when the British depart at midnight on June 30, supports the concepts of filial piety, consensus and the good of the community over the individual, the tenets of Asian values shared by Singapore's no-nonsense elder statemen Lee Kuan Yew.
"I don't believe in "Asian values'," Loh, 41, told Reuters in a recent interview.

"I believe that Asians have a distinctive culture and history but I get very upset when Asian governments use bits of history and culture to say Asian values mean Asians naturally accept authoritarianism," she said. It's a distorted argument."

Tung, who will be 60 this month, has stirred up a political storm in recent weeks by floating plans to amend Hong Kong's Public Order and Societies laws, to compel protesters to obtain police permission to demonstrate, and to prohibit foreign donations to local political groups.
Loh is typical of the younger generation of articulate, bilingual and self-confident young democrats coming of age at a particularly challenging time for Hong Kong.
About 200 demonstrators took to the streets on Sunday to oppose Tung's plans.

"Hong Kong people are not prepared to be pushed around any more. Hong Kong has changed a lot," said law professor Raymond Wacks, who has worked in Hong Kong for 14 years, observing the social changes and political liberalisation that have swept through the territory of 6.4 million people.
Tung has been forced to defend his plans in public.
In the past week he has appeared on the U.S. network ABC and on Cable News Network to pledge that Hong Kong would not see its cherished freedoms snuffed out.
Loh considers her generation to have fulfilled their parents' aspirations. "They wanted us to be able to compete with the west. That's why they educated us in the west.
"It doesn't make us less Asian, but it does give us a more global perspective."
It has also imbued them with democratic ideals and western liberal values more akin to those of outgoing governor Patten than incoming chief executive Tung.
The departing British will bequeath only limited democracy to their last outpost in Asia.
Last-minute reforms spearheaded by Patten succeeded in removing all appointed members from the legislature and broadening the electorate. But the cost was considerable.
An angry China responded with plans to dismantle the elected legislature returned in 1995 and replace it with an interim appointed body charged with drafting fresh electoral laws.
Loh will lose her seat. She plans to contest the 1998 polls.

Patten, a former Conservative Party chairman credited with masterminding the party's 1992 general election victory, is due to visit Britain later this month to discuss Hong Kong affairs with the incoming Labour Government.
A Conservative MP has urged Patten to return to British politics and lead the party. Patten said he was flattered but declined.
